newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin keeps up pressure on Russian parliament.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin keeps up pressure on Russian parliament.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin urged the opposition-dominated parliament on Monday to approve a more liberal tax code and big cuts in social spending, but a top communist shot back that "hot months" are ahead.

Yeltsin, who later this week heads for a summit of the Group of Seven leading industrialised nations in the United States, met both his first deputy prime ministers, Anatoly Chubais and Boris Nemtsov, to discuss various social and economic issues.

"Important decisions are expected this week from the State Duma (lower house of parliament) on a package of social measures and on the tax code," Yeltsin's press service said in a statement after the meeting.
The measures are due for debate on Tuesday and Thursday respectively.

"The president is closely following the deputies' examination of these issues," it said in remarks clearly aimed at keeping up the pressure on the communist-dominated Duma before it breaks for its summer recess on June 24.
The social package includes a clampdown on housing, transport and other benefits paid out to millions of pensioners, war veterans and other politically sensitive groups.
The new tax code, which already forms the basis of the government's 1998 budget plans, aims to simplify the country's notoriously cumbersome and convoluted fiscal system.

The government suffered a setback on Monday, however, when the Duma's budget committee issued a non-binding recommendation to the chamber rejecting the tax code in favour of more piecemeal legislation to address the most pressing problems.
The communist speaker of the Duma, Gennady Seleznyov, said the liberal team now in charge of economic policy could fan social tensions in Russia.

"Everything depends on the government. July, August -- these have to be hot months for the government, from the point of view of solving urgent problems that cannot wait until the autumn," Interfax news agency quoted Seleznyov as saying.
He also accused Chubais, a hate figure for the communists, of "lying" when he suggested that Russia could soon enter a period of economic stability.

Another item on the Duma's agenda this week is the government's plan to slash a fifth of budgeted spending in 1997, a total of 108 trillion roubles ($18.8 billion), to offset a big shortfall in tax revenues.

The Duma is angry about the cuts, saying they will hurt the poorest Russians during a continuing economic slump. But it wants to avoid a head-on clash with the government for fear of provoking Yeltsin into calling early parliamentary elections.
Last week parliament and the government set up a special commission to look in detail at where the cuts might fall. It has until Wednesday to draw up its recommendations.
A parliamentary source told Reuters that no concrete decisions had yet been made, but the commission was unlikely to approve cuts of more than 70 trillion roubles.

Chubais, who is also finance minister, has said that force of circumstance means the government will go ahead with the planned cuts regardless of parliament's decision, but he would prefer to win the Duma's backing.
The Kremlin has been using fear of an early Duma dissolution to cajole deputies into toeing the line, though the government is also known to be less than keen on early parliamentary elections.
"We are absolutely unwilling to dissolve them but if there is open sabotage, and open challenges, then we will have to think hard," one Kremlin official told Reuters.
Yeltsin's spokesman, Sergei Yastrzhembsky, told Itar-Tass news agency such talk was "idle chatter". He also denied reports Yeltsin had met Communist leader Gennady Zyuganov.

Aside from economic policy, Yeltsin and his parliamentary foes have clashed in recent days over such diverse issues as the return of art seized from Nazi Germany in World War Two and the possible burial of Lenin's mummified body.
